# The Mean Value Theorem

<!-- ::: {.callout-note}
## Companion reading
This lecture corresponds to C&J §2.8.h–i: the mean value theorem of differential calculus and its
proof by way of Rolle's theorem.
::: -->

## Local and Global Information

The derivative
$$
f'(x) = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}
$$
is a **local** quantity: it only depends on the values of $f$ in an arbitrarily small neighborhood
of $x$. A difference quotient
$$
\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a},
$$
on the other hand, compares the values of $f$ at two points that may be far apart, so it reflects
a **global** property of $f$. The Mean Value Theorem connects the two. It is the most important tool
for deriving *global* properties of a function from *local* properties of its derivative.

**Geometric picture.** The difference quotient $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ is the slope of the
**secant** through the points $(a,f(a))$ and $(b,f(b))$ of the graph of $f$. Imagine shifting this
secant parallel to itself, away from the graph. At some point $\xi$ between $a$ and $b$ the shifted
line will just touch the graph without crossing it: it becomes the **tangent** at $\xi$. (One such
point is the point of the graph that is farthest from the secant.) Since the tangent is parallel to
the secant, the two have the same slope:
$$
f'(\xi) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
$$

::: {#exr-mvt-fails}
Try to draw the graph of a function on $[a,b]$ for which there is **no** point $\xi\in(a,b)$ at which
the tangent is parallel to the secant. Is your function continuous? Does it have a tangent at every
point?
:::

## The Mean Value Theorem

::: {#thm-mvt}
## Mean Value Theorem
Suppose $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. Then there exists $\xi$ with
$a<\xi<b$ and
$$
f'(\xi) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
$$
:::

Equivalently, $f(b)-f(a) = f'(\xi)\,(b-a)$. The theorem asserts only that such a $\xi$ *exists*; it
says nothing about where in $(a,b)$ it lies, and there may be several such points. Note also that
$f$ must be continuous on the *closed* interval, but differentiability is only required on the
*open* interval: the derivative need not exist at the endpoints.

Why do we need to assume that $f'(x)$ exists for **all** $x\in(a,b)$? A single point of
non-differentiability is enough to break the theorem.

::: {#exm-abs-no-mvt}
\
Let $f(x) = \abs{x}$ on $[-1,1]$. Then $f$ is continuous on $[-1,1]$, and the secant has slope
$$
\frac{f(1)-f(-1)}{1-(-1)} = \frac{1-1}{2} = 0 .
$$
But $f'(x) = -1$ for $x<0$ and $f'(x)=1$ for $x>0$, while $f'(0)$ does not exist (the left- and
right-sided limits of the difference quotient are $-1$ and $1$). So there is no $\xi\in(-1,1)$ with
$f'(\xi)=0$. The graph has a corner at $0$, and no tangent is parallel to the secant.
:::

::: {#exm-driving}
## Driving
\
Suppose you drive for $2$ hours and end up $120$ miles from where you started. Let $s(t)$ be your
distance from the starting point at time $t\in[0,2]$. Assume that your movement is continuous and
that your velocity $s'(t)$ exists at all times. By @thm-mvt, there is a moment $\xi\in(0,2)$ at which
your velocity was
$$
s'(\xi) = \frac{s(2)-s(0)}{2-0} = \frac{120-0}{2-0} = 60 \text{ mph}.
$$
Here the numerator is a distance and the denominator a time. In particular, you cannot claim to
have driven at less than $50$ mph the whole time. On the other hand, the theorem does not tell us
*when* you were going exactly $60$ mph.
:::

## Rolle's Theorem

We prove the Mean Value Theorem by first establishing the special case of a horizontal secant.

::: {#thm-rolle}
## Rolle's Theorem
Suppose $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f(a)=f(b)=0$. Then there
exists $\xi$ with $a<\xi<b$ and
$$
f'(\xi) = 0.
$$
:::

This is the Mean Value Theorem with a horizontal tangent: if the graph of $f$ meets the $x$-axis at
$a$ and at $b$, it must have a horizontal tangent somewhere in between.

The proof rests on the following key fact, which we have used before (see @rem-darboux-informal)
and will prove later.

::: {#thm-evt}
## Extreme Value Theorem
A continuous function on a closed interval $[a,b]$ assumes a global maximum and a global minimum.
That is, there exist $M$ and $m$ such that
$$
m \le f(x) \le M \qquad\text{for all } x\in[a,b],
$$
and there are points $x_m, x_M\in[a,b]$ with $f(x_m)=m$ and $f(x_M)=M$.
:::

With this, we can prove @thm-rolle.

::: {.proof}
Let $m$ and $M$ be the minimum and maximum of $f$ on $[a,b]$ (@thm-evt). Since $f(a)=f(b)=0$, we
must have
$$
m \le 0 \le M .
$$

*Case $m = M = 0$.* Then $f(x)=0$ for all $x\in[a,b]$. Every difference quotient of $f$ is $0$, so
$f'(\xi) = 0$ for every $\xi\in(a,b)$, and we are done.

*Case $M>0$.* There exists $\xi\in[a,b]$ with $f(\xi)=M$. Since $f(a)=f(b)=0<M$, $\xi$ is an
**interior point**: $\xi\in(a,b)$. Since $f(x)\le M$ for all $x\in[a,b]$, we have
$$
f(\xi+h) - f(\xi) \le 0
$$
for all $h$ with $\xi+h\in[a,b]$, in particular for all small enough $\abs h$. Hence
$$
\frac{f(\xi+h)-f(\xi)}{h} \le 0 \quad\text{for } h>0,
\qquad\qquad
\frac{f(\xi+h)-f(\xi)}{h} \ge 0 \quad\text{for } h<0 .
$$
Since $f$ is differentiable at $\xi$, the limit
$$
\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(\xi+h)-f(\xi)}{h}
$$
exists, no matter from which direction $h\to0$. Letting $h\to0$ through positive values, the limit
is $\le0$; letting $h\to0$ through negative values, it is $\ge0$ (a limit of nonpositive numbers is
nonpositive; compare the argument at the end of the proof of @thm-ivt). Since the left-sided and the
right-sided limit agree (@def-one-sided-limits), we must have
$$
f'(\xi) = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(\xi+h)-f(\xi)}{h} = 0 .
$$

*Case $M=0$, $m<0$.* The same argument, applied at a point $\xi$ where $f$ attains its minimum $m$
(or the previous case applied to $-f$), gives $f'(\xi)=0$.
:::

::: {#rem-interior-extremum}
The proof shows more than Rolle's theorem: if $f$ attains a maximum or a minimum at an **interior**
point $\xi$ of an interval, and $f$ is differentiable at $\xi$, then $f'(\xi)=0$. The assumption
$f(a)=f(b)=0$ was only used to guarantee that an extremum occurs in the interior.
:::

## Proof of the Mean Value Theorem

To deduce @thm-mvt from @thm-rolle, we subtract the secant from $f$. Define
$$
\varphi(x) := f(x) - f(a) - \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\,(x-a).
$$
The secant through $(a,f(a))$ and $(b,f(b))$ is the line $y = f(a) + \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}(x-a)$, so
$\varphi(x)$ is the **vertical distance** between the point $(x,f(x))$ on the graph and the point of
the secant above (or below) $x$.

::: {.proof}
Plugging in the endpoints,
$$
\varphi(a) = f(a) - f(a) - 0 = 0,
\qquad
\varphi(b) = f(b) - f(a) - \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}(b-a) = 0 .
$$
The function $\varphi$ is of the form
$$
\varphi(x) = f(x) + c\,x + d,
\qquad\text{with constants}\quad
c = -\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}, \quad d = -f(a) + \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\,a .
$$
So $\varphi$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ (@cor-continuity-algebra), and since
$$
\frac{\varphi(x+h)-\varphi(x)}{h} = \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} + c ,
$$
it is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with
$$
\varphi'(x) = f'(x) + c .
$$
By @thm-rolle there exists $\xi$ with $a<\xi<b$ and $\varphi'(\xi)=0$. Hence
$$
f'(\xi) = -c = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} .
$$
:::

::: {#rem-rolle-general}
Applying @thm-mvt to a function with $f(a)=f(b)$ gives $f'(\xi)=0$. So Rolle's theorem holds more
generally whenever $f(a)=f(b)$, not only when both values are $0$.
:::

## Application: Lipschitz Continuity

::: {#def-lipschitz}
\
A function $f$ is **Lipschitz continuous** on an interval $I$ if there is a constant $L\ge0$ such that
$$
\abs{f(x)-f(y)} \le L\,\abs{x-y} \qquad\text{for all } x,y\in I .
$$
:::

In other words, all difference quotients $\frac{f(x)-f(y)}{x-y}$ of $f$ on $I$ are bounded in absolute
value by $L$: the secant slopes of $f$ cannot become arbitrarily steep. A Lipschitz continuous
function is continuous: given $\eps>0$, the choice $\delta=\eps/L$ (any $\delta$ if $L=0$) works in
@def-continuity at every point.

We say $f$ is **continuously differentiable** on $[a,b]$ if $f'$ exists on $[a,b]$ (as a one-sided
derivative at the endpoints) and $f'$ is continuous on $[a,b]$.

::: {#prp-c1-lipschitz}
\
Any function $f$ that is continuously differentiable on $[a,b]$ is Lipschitz continuous on $[a,b]$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Since $f'$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, it is bounded there by @thm-evt: there is $L$ with
$$
\abs{f'(x)} \le L \qquad\text{for all } x\in[a,b].
$$
Now let $a\le x<y\le b$. Then $f$ is continuous on $[x,y]$ and differentiable on $(x,y)$, so by
@thm-mvt there is $\xi\in(x,y)$ with
$$
\abs{f(y)-f(x)} = \abs{f'(\xi)\,(y-x)} = \abs{f'(\xi)}\,\abs{y-x} \le L\,\abs{y-x} .
$$
:::

The proof only used that $f'$ is bounded on $(a,b)$ (and that $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$), so this
weaker assumption is already enough.

::: {#exm-cube-root-not-lipschitz}
## Not every continuous function is Lipschitz continuous
\
Let $f(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}$ on $[-1,1]$. This function is continuous. But for $x\neq0$,
$$
\frac{f(x)-f(0)}{x-0} = \frac{x^{1/3}}{x} = x^{-2/3},
$$
which is **not bounded** near $0$: for $x = \frac1{n^3}$ it equals $n^2$. So no constant $L$ can
satisfy $\abs{f(x)-f(0)}\le L\abs{x-0}$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$. This does not contradict
@prp-c1-lipschitz: $f$ is not differentiable at $0$ — the graph has a vertical tangent there, and
$f'(x) = \frac13 x^{-2/3}$ is unbounded near $0$.
:::

## Summary

- The **Mean Value Theorem** (@thm-mvt): if $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
  $(a,b)$, then $f'(\xi) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ for some $\xi\in(a,b)$. Geometrically, some tangent
  is parallel to the secant. It turns local information (the derivative) into global information
  (difference quotients). For example, an average speed of $60$ mph forces a moment of speed exactly
  $60$ mph (@exm-driving).
- Differentiability at **every** interior point is needed: $\abs x$ on $[-1,1]$ has a corner and no
  horizontal tangent (@exm-abs-no-mvt).
- **Rolle's Theorem** (@thm-rolle) is the special case $f(a)=f(b)=0$. Its proof uses the **Extreme
  Value Theorem** (@thm-evt): $f$ attains a maximum or minimum at an interior point $\xi$, and there
  the right-sided difference quotients are $\le0$ and the left-sided ones $\ge0$ (or vice versa), so
  $f'(\xi)=0$ (@rem-interior-extremum).
- The Mean Value Theorem follows by applying Rolle's theorem to $\varphi(x) = f(x) - \big(\text{secant
  at } x\big)$, which vanishes at $a$ and $b$ and has $\varphi' = f' - \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$.
- **Application:** a continuously differentiable function on $[a,b]$ is **Lipschitz continuous**,
  $\abs{f(x)-f(y)}\le L\abs{x-y}$ with $L$ a bound for $\abs{f'}$ (@prp-c1-lipschitz). Continuous
  functions need not be Lipschitz: $\sqrt[3]{x}$ has unbounded difference quotients at $0$
  (@exm-cube-root-not-lipschitz).
